title: Simon and Jude (28 October)
hookLine: two little-known apostles; Jude is patron of hopeless cases

lines: A NIGHT OF PRAYER, THEN TWELVE NAMES.
cards: In Luke's Gospel, Jesus goes up a mountain, prays all night, and in the morning chooses twelve. Then the text simply lists them. Peter and Andrew, James and John, and on down.
Near the end come two names that slide past almost unnoticed: "Simon who is called Zelotes," and Jude, the brother of James. Then the list ends with Judas Iscariot, the traitor.
Two men chosen in that same morning light, and the Gospels give them barely a line apiece. The Church keeps their feast together.

teach.b: Start with Simon. The Gospels tell us almost one thing about him: a nickname. Luke calls him Zelotes, the zealot; Matthew and Mark call him the Cananean.
What it meant then, readers still discuss. It may mean a man of fierce zeal for God and his people. Some think it points to a group that wanted to throw off Roman rule.
Either way, Jesus chose a man with fire in him and put him in the same small band as Matthew, a publican who had sat at a tax table.
Whatever each thought of the other's past, they ended up walking the same roads and eating at the same table.
Now Jude. In John's Gospel, at the Last Supper, a Judas speaks up, and John is careful to add: not the Iscariot. He asks Jesus why he will show himself to them and not to the whole world.
It's a real question, and Jesus answers with love and the promise of a home. That's nearly all Jude says on the page.
Tradition says Simon and Jude later preached far to the east and died as martyrs, which is why they share a feast. Then something odd happened to Jude.
His name sounds like the betrayer's, and some say people avoided praying to him for that reason. So, the story goes, he became the saint you turn to last, when everything else has been tried.
Catholic devotion calls him the patron of hopeless cases, of lost causes.
The forgotten apostle became the one people remember when nobody else is left to ask.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saints Simon and Jude on 28 October, and Catholics pray to Saint Jude for desperate situations, sometimes in a novena.

o: a title for Jude, brother of James
the hill where the twelve were chosen

games.q: the forgotten apostles — tap the pairs.
p: a tax collector in the same band

John's Gospel says plainly: not the Iscariot.

games.q: you're Jude at the Last Supper. Jesus has said he will show himself to his friends. you're puzzled. what do you do?
o: stay quiet so you don't look slow.
ask him why he'll show himself to you and not to the world.
leave to tell the others outside.
games.why: Jude asks, and Jesus answers with love and a promise of a home with those who keep his word.

practice: Let one situation come to mind that seems past fixing: a friendship gone cold, someone's illness, a problem in the news that never moves. Don't solve it; just hold it, the way you'd hold something heavy with both hands.
If you pray, ask Saint Jude to pray for it, as some Catholics do; if not, keep it in mind with care, and let it be seen instead of filed away.

wordCard.voice: Zelotes, Luke's name for Simon the zealot. He and Jude, not the Iscariot, are two of the twelve whom tradition calls martyrs and whose feast the Church keeps together.

orig.note: Greek: zealot, one full of zeal; Luke's name for Simon.

carryVoice: Your line: the forgotten apostles. Barely a line apiece on the page, and still chosen. Until tomorrow.
